items.stem:
Read the following meme shared on a student forum, described in words.

[Image, top: a tiny kitten stares bravely at an enormous, overflowing laundry basket. Top text: 'ME IN SEPTEMBER: I'LL START MY IA EARLY THIS YEAR'.]
[Image, bottom: the same kitten, now buried under the laundry, only its ears showing. Bottom text: 'ME, 11:58 P.M. THE NIGHT BEFORE THE DEADLINE'.]

Explain what kind of identity the poster is performing, and how.
items.answer: The poster performs a relatable, chaotic student identity that invites others to say "same".

items.stem:
Read the following post from a travel blog written by a young backpacker in Vietnam.

Day 12. Hanoi. Honestly? I came for the Instagram shots – the lanterns, the train street, the egg coffee. What I got was Mrs Lan, who runs a tiny noodle stall and refused to let me pay because I tried (badly) to say 'thank you' in Vietnamese. Lesson learned: the best stuff here isn't on any list. #slowtravel

Evaluate what this text suggests about how digital communication is changing English.
items.answer: The informal register, minor sentences ("Day 12. Hanoi."), colloquial diction and hashtag reflect digital conventions; the attempted Vietnamese "thank you" shows language as a gesture of respect.

items.stem:
Read the following viral post shared on a messaging app.

SHARE BEFORE THEY DELETE THIS!!! My cousin's friend works at a hospital and says the new phone masts in our city are making people sick. The media won't report it. Why? Follow the money. Do your own research. [18.2k shares]

Evaluate how the text and its platform could contribute to misinformation.
items.answer: Features of misinformation: an urgent instruction to share, a claim of suppression ("they"), an unverifiable second-hand source, no data, and slogans that discredit experts; algorithms and forwarding reward emotional content, so it spreads faster than corrections.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Social media allows people to express their true identities."
items.answer: It enables expression but encourages performance; the "true" self online is always partly constructed.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: marginalised groups find voice and community; users can experiment with identity. Arguments against: personas are curated for approval; algorithms reward performance. Supported judgement: It enables expression but encourages performance; the "true" self online is always partly constructed.

items.stem: "Digital communication is making English simpler." Discuss.
items.answer: It is changing English rather than simplifying it, adding new resources for meaning.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: abbreviations and short messages dominate; punctuation is reduced. Arguments against: new conventions (emoji, ellipsis) add nuance; users manage many registers. Supported judgement: It is changing English rather than simplifying it, adding new resources for meaning. Markbands (10 marks): Markbands (criteria A–D). A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation of authorial choices; C Focus and organisation; D Language. Top band: an insightful, convincing interpretation supported by well-chosen references; perceptive analysis of how specific choices shape meaning and affect the audience; a sustained, coherent line of argument; precise, varied, register-appropriate academic language. Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.

items.stem: "Social media companies should be responsible for removing misinformation." Discuss.
items.answer: Platforms bear significant responsibility, but transparency and media literacy are needed alongside removal.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they profit from engagement; they have the tools to act. Arguments against: risks of censorship and errors; defining truth is contested.
